Photosynthesis.intro: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water. It is the foundation of almost all food chains.
Photosynthesis.mnemonic: Remember the photosynthesis equation: 'Carbon dioxide and Water, with Light and Chlorophyll, make Glucose and Oxygen.' CO₂ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂. Mnemonic: 'Clever Worms Light Candles, Growing Outdoors' — CO₂, Water, Light, Chlorophyll, Glucose, O₂. Or: 'Six Sixes make Twelve and Six' — 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.

sections.title: The Equation

callout.label: Word Equation
callout.text: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (requires light energy and chlorophyll)

points: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
Takes place in the chloroplasts
Chlorophyll absorbs light energy (mainly red and blue light, reflects green)

sections.title: Uses of Glucose
points: Respiration — releases energy for all cell processes
Making cellulose — for cell walls
Making amino acids — for proteins (combined with nitrates from soil)
Making starch — stored in leaves and stems
Making fats and oils — stored in seeds

sections.title: Adaptations of Leaves for Photosynthesis
sections.text: Leaf structure is closely linked to maximising the rate of photosynthesis:
points: Large surface area — maximises light absorption and CO₂ uptake
Thin — short diffusion distance for CO₂ to reach palisade cells
Chloroplasts in palisade cells — located near upper surface where light is strongest
Stomata on lower surface — allow CO₂ in and O₂ out; guard cells control opening
Vascular bundles (xylem + phloem) — supply water and remove glucose produced
Waxy cuticle — reduces water loss by evaporation while letting light through

keyTerms.def: Process using light energy to convert CO₂ and water into glucose and oxygen
Green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy
Organelle where photosynthesis takes place
The sugar produced by photosynthesis, used for respiration and building other molecules
The storage form of glucose in plants
A carbohydrate made from glucose that forms plant cell walls

examTips: Know the balanced symbol equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
Glucose is used for respiration FIRST — excess is stored as starch.
Do not say plants only photosynthesise and do not respire — plants respire ALL the time; in daylight, photosynthesis rate exceeds respiration rate so there is a net uptake of CO₂.
In questions about what glucose is used for, give at least THREE uses with examples.
commonMistakes: Saying plants only respire at night — they respire all the time, but in daylight photosynthesis rate > respiration rate.
Forgetting that amino acid production requires nitrogen from nitrates absorbed through roots — glucose alone is not enough.
Confusing the reactants and products — CO₂ and water are USED UP; glucose and oxygen are PRODUCED.
clozePassages: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants make their own food using light energy. The equation is: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen. Chlorophyll in the chloroplasts absorbs light energy to power the reaction. Carbon dioxide enters through stomata and water is absorbed through roots. Oxygen is released as a by-product and glucose is used for energy or converted to other molecules.

Photosynthesis occurs in two main stages. In the light-dependent reactions, light energy is used to split water molecules, releasing oxygen and producing ATP. In the light-independent reactions (the Calvin cycle), carbon dioxide is fixed using ATP to produce glucose. Both stages take place inside chloroplasts. The rate of photosynthesis can be measured by the rate of oxygen production.

Glucose produced by photosynthesis has several uses in the plant. It can be used in respiration to release energy. It can be converted to starch for storage, cellulose for cell walls, or proteins for growth and repair. It can also be converted to lipids for storage in seeds. The rate of photosynthesis can be increased by providing more light, more CO₂, or a warmer temperature.

Limiting Factors.intro: The rate of photosynthesis is controlled by limiting factors — the factor in shortest supply that restricts the rate. Understanding these is essential for B4.
Limiting Factors.mnemonic: Remember the three limiting factors: 'LCT' — Light intensity, CO₂ concentration, Temperature. Or picture a plant trying to photosynthesize at maximum rate needing all three topped up like a three-legged stool — if any one leg is too short (limiting), the whole stool (photosynthesis rate) falls. For the inverse square law: 'Double distance = Quarter light' — if you move twice as far away, you get only a quarter of the light.

sections.title: The Three Limiting Factors
points: Light intensity — more light = faster photosynthesis (up to a point)
CO₂ concentration — more CO₂ = faster photosynthesis (up to a point)
Temperature — higher temp = faster (up to ~40°C), then enzymes denature and rate drops

sections.title: Inverse Square Law
sections.text: Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source:

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: Light intensity ∝ 1/d² — if you double the distance, light intensity drops to a quarter.

sections.title: Commercial Greenhouses
points: Artificially increase CO₂ levels (gas burners)
Provide artificial lighting
Control temperature
This maximises photosynthesis rate for crop production

sections.title: Interpreting Limiting Factor Graphs
sections.text: AQA often shows graphs of photosynthesis rate vs one factor — you must be able to explain the shape:
points: Rising section — the factor on the x-axis is limiting; increasing it increases the rate
Plateau (flat section) — another factor has become limiting; increasing x-axis factor has no more effect
Temperature graph — sudden drop after optimum — enzyme denaturation; active site changes shape permanently
CO₂ graph — plateau — light or temperature is now limiting, not CO₂
Light graph — plateau — CO₂ or temperature is now limiting
Practical tip — in pondweed experiments, count bubbles (O₂ produced) per minute as a measure of photosynthesis rate

keyTerms.def: The factor in shortest supply that determines the rate of a process
Light intensity is proportional to 1/d² — doubling distance quarters intensity
The temperature at which enzymes work fastest — above this, denaturation causes rate to fall
Irreversible change in enzyme shape caused by high temperature or extreme pH
The light intensity at which the rate of photosynthesis equals the rate of respiration in a plant

examTips: In graph questions, the plateau is caused by a DIFFERENT factor becoming limiting — not the factor on the x-axis.
Temperature affects enzymes — above optimum they denature, causing rate to drop sharply.
For inverse square law calculations: light intensity = 1/d². If distance doubles (×2), intensity = 1/4 (×0.25).
In greenhouse questions, always explain WHY each factor is controlled and the economic benefit — more crop yield = more profit.
commonMistakes: Saying light is always the limiting factor — any of the three can be limiting depending on conditions.
Forgetting that increasing CO₂ beyond a certain point has no further effect if light or temperature is limiting.
Saying enzymes are 'killed' at high temperatures — they are 'denatured'; the active site changes shape permanently.
clozePassages: The rate of photosynthesis can be limited by three main factors: light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, and temperature. A limiting factor is the factor that is in shortest supply and therefore controls the rate of the reaction. Increasing light intensity increases the rate until another factor becomes limiting. This is why commercial greenhouses control all three factors to maximise crop growth.

Light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis because light provides the energy needed to drive the reaction. As light intensity increases, the rate increases until another factor becomes limiting. Carbon dioxide concentration also limits the rate — increasing CO₂ increases the rate up to a point. In greenhouses, CO₂ is sometimes pumped in and artificial lighting used to maintain high rates of photosynthesis.

Temperature affects the rate of photosynthesis because enzymes control the reactions. As temperature increases, reaction rates increase up to an optimum temperature. Above this temperature, the enzymes become denatured and the rate falls. In commercial greenhouses, temperature is carefully controlled using heaters. Providing optimum levels of light, CO₂, and temperature maximises yield and profit.

Aerobic Respiration.intro: Aerobic respiration is the process of releasing energy from glucose using oxygen. It occurs in the mitochondria and is the main way cells get energy.
Aerobic Respiration.mnemonic: Remember the aerobic respiration equation: 'Glucose and Oxygen make Carbon dioxide, Water, and Energy'. C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. The reverse of photosynthesis! Remember: aerobic respiration is the OPPOSITE equation to photosynthesis — reactants and products swap. Or: 'GOod CaWfee Energises' — Glucose, Oxygen → CO₂, Water, Energy.

sections.title: The Equation

callout.label: Word Equation
callout.text: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy released)

points: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O
Occurs in the mitochondria
Releases energy as ATP
Continuous process in all living cells

sections.title: Uses of Energy
points: Muscle contraction
Building larger molecules (proteins, DNA)
Active transport
Maintaining body temperature (mammals and birds)

sections.title: Aerobic vs Anaerobic Respiration
sections.text: It is essential to be able to compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration:
points: Aerobic — uses oxygen: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water; produces large amounts of ATP
Anaerobic (animals): glucose → lactic acid; produces much less ATP; no oxygen needed
Anaerobic (yeast/plants): glucose → ethanol + CO₂; produces much less ATP; no oxygen needed
Location: aerobic respiration mainly in mitochondria; anaerobic respiration in cytoplasm
Efficiency: aerobic produces up to 38 ATP per glucose molecule; anaerobic produces only 2 ATP per glucose — aerobic is approximately 19 times more efficient

keyTerms.def: Releasing energy from glucose using oxygen; produces CO₂ and water
The molecule that stores and transfers energy in cells
Organelles where aerobic respiration takes place
The sugar used as the main fuel for cellular respiration
The rate at which chemical reactions occur in the body; increases during exercise
The first stage of respiration; splits glucose into pyruvate in the cytoplasm

examTips: Respiration releases energy — it is not the same as breathing (which is ventilation).
Aerobic respiration is more efficient than anaerobic — produces more ATP per glucose.
Do not confuse respiration (releases energy in cells) with breathing (moves air in and out of lungs) — they are completely different processes.
For 'why do cells with more mitochondria respire faster' questions: more mitochondria = more sites for aerobic respiration = more ATP produced per unit time.
commonMistakes: Confusing respiration (cellular process) with breathing (gas exchange).
Forgetting respiration happens in ALL living cells, all the time — not just during exercise.
Writing the equation backwards — oxygen is a REACTANT, not a product of aerobic respiration.
clozePassages: Aerobic respiration is the process of releasing energy from glucose using oxygen. The word equation is: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy). It takes place mainly in the mitochondria. The energy released is used for movement, growth, maintaining body temperature, and active transport. Aerobic respiration releases much more energy than anaerobic respiration.

Aerobic respiration occurs in several stages. Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm and splits glucose into pyruvate. The pyruvate enters the mitochondria where it is broken down further in the Krebs cycle, releasing carbon dioxide and transferring energy to ATP. The final stage, oxidative phosphorylation, uses oxygen and produces most of the ATP. Overall, aerobic respiration produces up to 38 ATP molecules per glucose.

The products of aerobic respiration are carbon dioxide and water. Carbon dioxide is transported in the blood plasma and breathed out via the lungs. Water is used in metabolic reactions or excreted. The energy released is used to make ATP (adenosine triphosphate), which acts as an energy currency in the cell. ATP can be broken down to release energy wherever it is needed in the cell.

Anaerobic Respiration.intro: When oxygen is not available, cells can still release energy through anaerobic respiration — but less efficiently. The products are different depending on whether it's in animals or plants/yeast.
Anaerobic Respiration.mnemonic: Remember the two types of anaerobic respiration: 'Animals make Lactic acid; Yeast makes Ethanol (and CO₂)'. Think: 'Animals Lactic — ALL'. 'Yeast EthanoL — YEL'. Or use a rhyme: 'In muscles lactic acid makes you ache, in yeast and bread dough it makes it bake' — lactic acid in animals, ethanol + CO₂ in yeast/bread-making.

sections.title: In Animals (muscles)

callout.label: Equation
callout.text: Glucose → lactic acid (+ small amount of energy)

points: Occurs during intense exercise when oxygen cannot be delivered fast enough
Lactic acid builds up in muscles — causes fatigue and pain
Oxygen debt — extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down lactic acid

sections.title: In Plants and Yeast

callout.label: Equation
callout.text: Glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide (+ small amount of energy)

points: Called fermentation
Used in brewing (alcohol production) and bread-making (CO₂ causes dough to rise)
Yeast is a microorganism that can respire both aerobically and anaerobically

sections.title: Oxygen Debt and Recovery
sections.text: After intense exercise, the body must remove the lactic acid that has built up:
points: Oxygen debt definition — the extra volume of oxygen consumed after exercise, above resting levels, to break down lactic acid
Lactic acid removal — transported in blood to the liver; oxidised back to glucose using oxygen
Why you keep breathing hard after exercise — extra oxygen is needed to repay the oxygen debt
Heart rate stays elevated — to deliver oxygen to the liver to oxidise lactic acid
Complete oxidation — lactic acid → CO₂ + H₂O (using oxygen); this releases more energy and fully disposes of the lactic acid

keyTerms.def: Releasing energy from glucose without oxygen — less efficient than aerobic
Product of anaerobic respiration in animal cells; causes muscle fatigue
Anaerobic respiration in plants and yeast producing ethanol and CO₂
The extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down lactic acid
Alcohol produced by yeast during anaerobic respiration (fermentation)
The bursting of a cell — in respiration context, the breakdown of glucose molecules

examTips: In animals: glucose → lactic acid. In plants/yeast: glucose → ethanol + CO₂.
Anaerobic releases MUCH less energy than aerobic — always state this.
For oxygen debt questions: state what lactic acid is, where it goes (to the liver), and what happens to it (oxidised back to glucose or CO₂ + H₂O).
Fermentation has industrial applications — use brewing (alcohol) and baking (CO₂ raises dough) as specific examples.
commonMistakes: Using the wrong products — animals make lactic acid; yeast/plants make ethanol and CO₂.
Saying anaerobic respiration uses oxygen — it does not, that's the whole point.
Forgetting that lactic acid is removed by being oxidised in the liver — students often say it is 'broken down in muscles'.
clozePassages: Anaerobic respiration occurs when there is insufficient oxygen for aerobic respiration. In animals, glucose is converted to lactic acid, releasing a small amount of energy. In yeast and plant cells, glucose is converted to ethanol and carbon dioxide. Anaerobic respiration releases far less energy than aerobic respiration as glucose is only partially broken down.

During intense exercise, muscles may respire anaerobically producing lactic acid. This causes muscle fatigue and the burning sensation felt during hard exercise. The build-up of lactic acid creates an oxygen debt — the extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down the lactic acid. Lactic acid is transported to the liver where it is converted back to glucose during recovery.

Fermentation is anaerobic respiration in yeast and bacteria. Yeast converts glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide. This process is exploited in brewing to make alcoholic drinks and in baking, where the carbon dioxide produced causes bread to rise. The equation is: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide. Fermentation stops when the ethanol concentration becomes too high for the yeast to survive.

Response to Exercise.intro: During exercise, the body must respond quickly to deliver more oxygen and glucose to muscles and remove waste products. Understanding these physiological responses is required for B4.
Response to Exercise.mnemonic: Remember the body's responses to exercise: 'HB-GD': Heart rate up, Breathing rate up, Glycogen broken down to glucose, blood vessels Dilate. Or imagine a car accelerating: 'Rev the engine (heart), open the air vents (breathe more), use the fuel tank (glycogen), open the fuel lines wider (dilate blood vessels)'.

sections.title: Immediate Responses to Exercise
points: Heart rate increases — pumps blood faster to deliver O₂ and glucose to muscles
Breathing rate increases — takes in more O₂ and expels CO₂ faster
Breathing depth increases — larger tidal volume
Blood vessels dilate — more blood to working muscles
Glycogen → glucose — stored glycogen in muscles is converted to glucose for respiration

sections.title: Oxygen Debt
sections.text: If exercise is too intense, anaerobic respiration occurs and lactic acid builds up. After exercise, extra oxygen is needed to break down the lactic acid.

callout.label: Oxygen Debt
callout.text: After exercise, you continue breathing heavily — this extra oxygen is used to break down lactic acid into CO₂ and water (aerobic oxidation of lactic acid).

sections.title: Long-Term Effects of Regular Exercise
sections.text: Regular exercise causes lasting adaptations that make the body more efficient:
points: Stronger heart muscle — larger stroke volume; can pump more blood per beat; lower resting heart rate
More capillaries in muscles — improved oxygen and glucose delivery to muscle cells
More mitochondria in muscle cells — more sites for aerobic respiration; muscles can work harder before going anaerobic
Increased lung capacity — more oxygen can be taken in per breath
Improved removal of waste — CO₂ and lactic acid removed more efficiently, delaying fatigue

keyTerms.def: The storage form of glucose in muscles and liver
Extra oxygen needed after anaerobic exercise to remove lactic acid
The volume of air breathed in or out in one breath
The volume of blood pumped by the heart per beat
Widening of blood vessels, increasing blood flow to muscles during exercise
Hormone released during exercise that increases heart rate and prepares the body for action

examTips: Know that glycogen is the stored form of glucose — it is broken down during exercise.
Oxygen debt explains why you keep breathing hard after stopping exercise.
For 'explain why heart rate increases during exercise' — say: muscles need more oxygen and glucose for aerobic respiration; heart rate increases to deliver these faster and remove CO₂ more quickly.
Heart rate and breathing rate BOTH increase — and BOTH stay elevated after exercise to repay the oxygen debt.
commonMistakes: Saying heart rate increases to supply more oxygen only — it also supplies more glucose and removes CO₂ and lactic acid.
Forgetting that glycogen is broken down to glucose during exercise.
Saying exercise stops when oxygen runs out — in fact, anaerobic respiration kicks in to allow exercise to continue, but lactic acid builds up causing fatigue.
clozePassages: During exercise, muscles need more energy from respiration. To supply more oxygen and glucose to muscles, heart rate increases and blood is diverted from the gut to the muscles. Breathing rate and depth also increase to take in more oxygen and remove carbon dioxide faster. These changes are controlled by the nervous system and hormones such as adrenaline.

When exercise intensity exceeds what aerobic respiration can supply, muscles switch to anaerobic respiration to produce extra energy. This produces lactic acid which causes muscle fatigue. After exercise, the body continues to take in extra oxygen to repay the oxygen debt — the extra oxygen needed to break down lactic acid and restore normal conditions.

Regular exercise has many health benefits. It strengthens the heart muscle, reducing the risk of heart disease. It increases lung capacity and improves oxygen delivery to muscles. It increases muscle mass and metabolic rate. Exercise also reduces the risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and some cancers. The body adapts over time, becoming more efficient at delivering oxygen and removing waste products.
